draft.title: Voice as a literary device
card: Voice is the personality that comes through a text's narration or speaker. It comes from choices a writer makes again and again, not from one striking line.
Diction
the words chosen. Slang, formal terms or plain words each suggest a different speaker.
Rhythm
the pattern of sentence length and sound. Short, clipped sentences feel different from long, winding ones.
Attitude

the speaker's stance towards the subject, such as wry, angry, tender or doubtful. When these choices stay consistent, the voice is distinct and shapes how a reader feels, such as whether they trust or pity the speaker.
draft.remember: Voice is the personality of a narrator or speaker, built from repeated choices in diction, rhythm and attitude.

a.q: A writer wants a narrator's personality to come through clearly. Which approach would work best?
opts: Keeping a steady style of diction, rhythm and attitude
Changing the speaker's style in every paragraph
Using one very unusual word near the start
Switching to a new attitude for each new idea
a.why: Voice comes from choices repeated across a piece, so consistency lets the reader recognise one speaker. One unusual word is a single choice, so it cannot build a voice on its own.
a.clue: Think about what makes a speaker sound like the same person throughout.

b.q: A narrator in a short story describes a storm in three very short sentences, one after another. Which part of voice does this mainly show?
opts: Rhythm
Diction
Attitude
Audience
b.why: Rhythm is the pattern of sentence length and sound, so a run of short sentences shapes the rhythm. Diction is tempting, but it is about which words are chosen, and the question says nothing about the words themselves.
b.clue: Imagine reading the opening aloud and notice what you hear.

a.best: Keeping a steady style of diction, rhythm and attitude

proposal.title: Voice as a literary device
card: Voice is the personality that comes through a text's narration or speaker. It is built from choices a writer makes across a text, not from one striking line.
Diction
the words chosen. Slang, formal terms or plain words each suggest a different speaker.
Rhythm
the pattern of sentence length and sound. Short, clipped sentences feel different from long, winding ones.
Attitude

the speaker's stance towards the subject, such as wry (dry and mocking), angry, tender or doubtful. This shapes how readers feel: a wry voice may make them smile, a tender one may make them pity the speaker.
proposal.remember: Diction, rhythm and attitude build a voice, and voice shapes how readers feel about what they read.

a.q: A narrator says: "Sure, the bus was late again. Shocking, I know." What effect does this voice most likely have?
opts: It suggests a dry, mocking narrator the reader may smile at
It suggests a frightened narrator the reader may worry about
It suggests a formal narrator who keeps readers distant
It suggests a tender narrator the reader may feel sorry for
a.why: The narrator pretends to be shocked by something ordinary, which is a wry, mocking attitude, so a reader may smile. The casual words like "Sure" rule out a formal voice, and nothing in the line shows fear or tenderness.
a.clue: Is the narrator really shocked by a late bus?

b.clue: Imagine reading the passage aloud and notice what you hear.
